newsitem.title: UK: More links found to genes and diabetes.
newsitem.headline: More links found to genes and diabetes.

text.p: Italian researchers said on Friday they had shed more light on the question of how important genes are to developing diabetes with a study showing that children of Sardinian heritage are especially prone to the disease, wherever they live.
Scientists are finding more and more genes linked to the various forms of diabetes, but there are also strong indications that environment, especially diet, plays a big role.

Reporting in the Lancet medical journal, Sergio Muntoni of the Centre for Metabolic Diseases in Cagliari and colleagues said they looked at cases of insulin-dependent diabetes on the Mediterranean island of Sardinia and among Sardinian immigrants to mainland Italy.
Sardinia has the second-highest rate of childhood-onset insulin-dependent diabetes in the world, with 30 cases in 100,000 people every year.
Nearby Lazio on the Italian mainland has a low rate of 6.5 per 100,000. The two regions are similar in terms of lifestyle and culture.
But Muntoni's group found that children born to Sardinian parents who had moved to Lazio developed diabetes four times as often as children born to Lazio natives.
"Children of Sardinian heritage born in Lazio have the same incidence as the population of origin, which is genetically prone to the disease," they wrote.
Those born to couples made up of one Sardinian and one Lazio native got diabetes twice as often.

"The fact that children born in Lazio of couples with one Sardinian partner have a rate half that of Sardinians but double that of the indigenous population emphasises the supremacy of genetic features over the environment," they concluded.
